title: The Difficulty of the Guardian Crossword, 1930 to 2026
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Daisy Christodoulou applies Comparative Judgement, the assessment-research methodology her company No More Marking uses to grade GCSE mock exams, to a genuinely novel question: has the Guardian's cryptic crossword grown easier or harder across nearly a century, from 1930 to 2026? Expert judges made 8,310 head-to-head difficulty comparisons across 465 clues sampled from every era, reaching a reliability coefficient of 0.82, strong enough to trust the resulting difficulty scale, and the answer was a real but modest decline in difficulty, with the 1930s hardest and the 1980s easiest, before setters like Araucaria and Paul began tightening the screws again in the 1990s and 2000s. The more interesting finding, Christodoulou argues, is not the overall trend but what actually drove difficulty in each era: 1930s-1950s clues were hard largely because they were quotations and general-knowledge definitions with no wordplay at all, forms that would be considered illegitimate in a modern cryptic crossword under the Ximenean rules codified in 1966, whereas modern difficulty comes from the lateral-thinking demand of parsing wordplay layered on top of cultural knowledge. The study's design honestly confronts its own methodological complication: judges disagreed sharply on whether older, non-cryptic clue types should even count as "harder," and one judge's explicit rating choice was flagged as mechanically guaranteeing part of the study's apparent difficulty trend.
points: The study achieved an unusually high reliability coefficient (0.82 across 8,310 pairwise decisions on 465 clues), giving the difficulty-over-time finding real statistical weight rather than resting on a small or noisy sample.

Christodoulou transparently surfaces a methodological confound rather than hiding it: judge Ashley Knowles admitted his own rule (rating all pre-Ximenean definitional clues as automatically easier than any cryptic clue) would 'guarantee an apparent increase in difficulty over time' regardless of the true pattern, a rare instance of a researcher naming how her own judges' decision rules shape the result.

The finding that clue difficulty across nine decades never actually tracks the zeitgeist, a 1933 clue references an already-decommissioned technology, a 1970 clue references a 50-year-old cricketer, a 2025 clue references 1970s-era Scooby Doo, shows the crossword has always deliberately drawn on settled cultural memory rather than current events.

The most substantive conclusion reframes what 'difficulty' even means across eras: 1930s-1950s clues were hard because they were undisguised quotations and general-knowledge definitions with zero wordplay, a form the modern Ximenean cryptic rules would now disqualify entirely, meaning the puzzle's difficulty didn't just decrease, its source fundamentally changed.
quotes: I presented the clues with the solution to expert judges, with the simple instruction to choose: The harder clue?

I decided to rate all such clues as easier than any cryptic clue, and my responses will therefore automatically anchor the bottom end of the regression and guarantee an apparent increase in difficulty over time, even though there's an argument that cryptic clues are actually easier for an experienced solver than plain definitional clues.
Remarkably, the reliability of the judging was high at 0.82 after 8,310 decisions on 465 clues revealing that generally there was good consensus on the perceived difficulty of the clues.
The hardest decade was perceived by judges to be the 1930s and the 1980s the easiest. Over time we see a real (statistically significant) but modest fall in difficulty.

A quote from Henry V, a biblical figure and a quote from a Victorian poem all feature in the hardest clues from that period, none of which would qualify today as cryptic as they do not feature any form of wordplay.

My question when I began this study was whether the Guardian Crossword has grown easier over time, and the answer, statistically speaking, is yes, it has. The answer, however, turns out to be less interesting than the transition in the cluing that is evident in the sources of difficulty.
